To argue that moral responsibility requires a meaningful conception of agency irreducible to causal-mechanical description begins with the observation that ascriptions of moral responsibility presuppose that agents could have done otherwise. This counterfactual competence condition is not merely a logical flourish but a deeply embedded feature of our ordinary practice of holding one another accountable. When we judge that someone acted wrongly and deserves blame, we implicitly assume that, at the moment of action, they possessed the capacity to select a different course of conduct. Deterministic causal chains, however, represent every action as the necessary output of prior events together with laws of nature. Within such a closed mechanical framework, the notion that an agent could have done otherwise is strictly false unless one smuggles in a normative surplus that the mechanistic description itself does not contain. A physical system unfolding deterministically has no options; it simply follows its trajectory. To say of a person within that system that they could have refrained from acting as they did requires importing evaluative standards—considerations of reasons, capacities, or alternative possibilities—that have no analogue in the causal-mechanical vocabulary of forces, particles, or neural firings. The deterministic description exhausts the facts about motion and change but leaves no conceptual room for genuine alternative possibilities, and without such possibilities, the ground for moral responsibility dissolves.

The irreducibility of responsible agency becomes even clearer when we examine the reactive attitudes—resentment, indignation, gratitude—that structure our interpersonal moral lives. These attitudes are not mere behavioral dispositions or cognitive judgments about causal regularity; they are responses to agents as sources of reasons-responsive action. When we feel resentment toward someone who has wronged us, we are not simply registering that their behavior was caused by prior events in a way that could be predicted. Rather, we are responding to the person as one who could have recognized and responded to the relevant moral reasons but failed to do so. Gratitude, similarly, is not a calculation of beneficial causal effects but an appreciation of another’s goodwill and deliberate choice to act for our sake. These reactive attitudes become unintelligible or even pathological if we try to reduce the agent to a node in a causal network. A stone that rolls down a hill and injures us does not provoke resentment; a machine programmed to insult us does not elicit indignation in the full interpersonal sense. What distinguishes the person from the merely mechanical is that we interpret the person as an originator of action in light of reasons, not merely as the passive terminus of a causal chain. The reactive attitudes thus presuppose a framework of agency that treats persons as capable of stepping back from their desires and impulses, deliberating about what they ought to do, and acting on the basis of that deliberation. This framework is normative through and through; it cannot be translated into the language of cause and effect without losing what makes the attitudes appropriate or inappropriate in the first place.

Compatibilist attempts to reconcile moral responsibility with determinism succeed, if at all, only by shifting the conceptual target rather than preserving what matters about agency. The classic compatibilist move is to redefine “could have done otherwise” in dispositional terms: an agent could have done otherwise if they would have done otherwise had they desired or chosen differently, or if nothing external constrained them. Such redefinitions preserve the linguistic form of responsibility attribution while abandoning its normative substance. Under the dispositional reading, an agent in a deterministic world is said to have the capacity to act otherwise in exactly the same sense that a sugar cube is said to be soluble in water even if it never touches water. But this analogy fails precisely because moral responsibility requires more than a hypothetical conditional about what would happen under counterfactual circumstances. When we hold someone responsible for a malicious act, we are not merely noting that if their desires had been different, they would have acted differently. We are asserting that at the actual moment of choice, faced with the actual reasons and alternatives, they genuinely could have refrained. The deterministic picture denies that such genuine possibility exists, because every mental state and action is fixed by prior causes. The compatibilist’s dispositional analysis changes the subject from actual alternative possibilities to hypothetical ones, from what the agent could have done in the actual situation to what they would have done in a different situation. This maneuver may satisfy a certain logical consistency, but it evacuates responsibility of the very feature that underwrites our reactive attitudes: the sense that the agent was a genuine source of their action, facing real alternatives that were not closed off by the inexorable march of prior causes. What remains is a thin, behavioral notion of responsibility that no longer answers to the normative demands of blame, praise, resentment, or gratitude. Thus, any meaningful conception of moral responsibility requires an understanding of agency as something more than a node in a causal-mechanical order—specifically, as a source of reasons-responsive action whose counterfactual competence is irreducible to deterministic description.
